newsitem.title: CANADA: FOCUS-Canadian unveils plan to stem losses.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Canadian unveils plan to stem losses.

text.p: Canadian Airlines Corp, struggling to survive amid heavy losses, said on Friday it would add capacity on foreign flights, seek wage cuts from employees and ask for concessions from its U.S. shareholder, AMR Corp.

Canadian, which said its year-to-date financial results were much worse than expected, added it could face a serious cash crunch in the first quarter of 1997 and that a string of losses threatened its survival.
"Canadian has had a history of chronic losses. We have to address it and we are addressing it," Benson told a packed news conference at the company's head office.

Benson said the moves, which require approval from Canadian's unions and AMR, would slowly bring the carrier to profitability without revenue growth by adding C$800 million ($600 million) to its bottom line over four years. The details were not negotiable, he said.
But the plan quickly hit turbulence with the company's unions, the biggest of which said it would reject attempts to cut its members' pay after numerous wage concessions in the last few years.

"This is deplorable. Basically, we are being asked to tell (union members) that once again you have to buy your jobs," an angry Davie Ritchie, vice-president of District Lodge 721 of the International Association of Machinists, told reporters. We are not prepared to do that."
The IAM represents represents 5,300 of Canadian's 12,000 unionized workers.
The carrier this year struck deals with all but one of its unions aimed at saving C$125 million ($94 million) a year in labor costs. The IAM agreement saved the airline C$34 million ($26 million)
The Canadian Auto Workers, which represents the airline's 3,700 passenger and reservation agents, also said Friday that wage rollbacks were "no solution."
Canadian, which has not posted an annual profit this decade, said it lost C$49 million ($36.7 million) in the first nine months of 1996 versus a year-ago loss of C$65.4 million ($49.1 million).

Calgary-based Canadian -- Canada's second-biggest airline -- said it had C$110.8 million ($92.1 million) in cash on hand at the end of the third quarter. But continued operating losses and high debt repayments in the next six months could wipe out reserves by the first quarter of 1997.
The airline was poised for a 1996 loss that will be less than last year, but still "significant," Benson said. Canadian lost C$195 million ($146 million) in 1995.
Under the proposal, Canadian would double its service to the United States and boost Asian service by 20 percent, in moves that would take advantage of its expanded Vancouver hub.
In Canada, where the carrier faces brutal price competition from no-frills upstarts Greyhound Air and WestJet Airlines, Canadian will cut capacity by 11 percent.
Canadian said it also planned to make better use of its smaller Canadian Regional jets to service domestic destinations in order to wring more much-needed cost savings from its fleet.
Up to 250 jobs could be eliminated under the plan, but most positions would be cut through attrition, the company said.

Canadian's survival plan also envisages saving C$70 million ($53 million) by asking AMR Corp, which holds 33 percent of the airline, to reduce fees for overhead, reservation services and other payments. Fort Worth-based AMR, the parent of American Airlines, receives about $100 million each year from Canadian.
AMR, which is considering a major writedown of its Canadian Airlines investment, said it remained committed to its stake would consider "all reasonable Canadian requests for assistance."
Canadian said it would ask employees and unions to indicate their support for the strategy by the end of this month.
